q: How many bones are there in the typical adult human body?
note: A newborn has considerably more, because many bones start out as separate pieces and fuse together during childhood.

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
note: Its outer layer completely replaces itself roughly once a month.

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
note: The two atria on top collect incoming blood and the two ventricles below pump it back out.

q: Which type of blood cell carries oxygen around the body?
note: They do it using hemoglobin, the iron-rich protein that also gives blood its color.

q: Which vitamin does the body manufacture when skin is exposed to sunlight?
note: It helps the body absorb calcium, which is why a serious shortage causes the bone disease rickets.

q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
note: It is also the strongest, and it accounts for roughly a quarter of a person's height.

q: What is the medical term for the kneecap?
note: It is the body's largest sesamoid bone, meaning it grew inside a tendon rather than joining two bones together.

q: Which organ produces the hormone insulin?
note: Insulin comes from small clusters of cells inside it called the islets of Langerhans.

q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
note: It sits in the middle ear, is only about three millimeters long, and is shaped like a stirrup.

q: Which colored part of the eye controls the size of the pupil?
note: Its ring of muscle opens and closes the pupil much like the aperture of a camera.

q: What is the medical name for the voice box?
note: It holds the vocal folds, which vibrate as air is pushed up between them.

q: What is the largest artery in the human body?
note: It carries freshly oxygenated blood out of the heart's left ventricle and arches over the top of the heart.

q: How many pairs of ribs does a typical adult human have?
note: The bottom two pairs are called floating ribs because they attach to the spine but not to the breastbone.

q: A lack of which vitamin causes the disease scurvy?
note: Naval surgeon James Lind showed in 1747 that citrus fruit could cure it, long before anyone understood why.

q: What is the pale yellow liquid that blood cells float in called?
note: It makes up a little over half of blood by volume and is itself mostly water.

q: Which pea-sized gland at the base of the brain is often called the body's master gland?
note: It releases hormones that tell the thyroid, the adrenal glands and others when to do their jobs.

q: Which is the only bone in the human body that is not joined to any other bone?
note: It sits in the throat held by muscle and ligament alone, and it anchors the tongue.

q: What is the spiral, fluid-filled part of the inner ear that turns sound into nerve signals?
note: Its name comes from the Greek word for snail, which is more or less exactly what it looks like.

q: What is the clear liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord called?
note: The brain effectively floats in it, which cuts its apparent weight to a small fraction of the real thing.

q: What is the longest and thickest nerve in the human body?
note: It runs from the lower back down through each leg, and pressure on it is what produces sciatica.

q: What is the largest animal on Earth?
note: A newborn calf is already around seven meters long and puts on weight faster than almost any other animal.

q: What is the fastest land animal?
note: It accelerates like a sports car but can only hold a full sprint for about half a minute before overheating.

q: Which gas do plants take in from the air in order to make their food?
note: It enters through tiny pores on the leaves called stomata, and oxygen leaves the same way as a by-product.

q: How many legs does a spider have?
note: That is one of the things that separates spiders from insects, which have six.

q: What is the tallest living land animal?
note: Its towering neck contains exactly the same number of vertebrae as a human neck: seven.

q: Which is the only mammal capable of true, sustained flight?
note: Other so-called flying mammals, such as flying squirrels, can only glide.

q: What is the collective name for a group of lions?
note: A pride is normally built around a group of related females, while the males come and go.

q: Which family of birds is able to fly backwards?
note: They can also hover on the spot, beating their wings dozens of times every second.

q: Which is the largest of the big cats?
note: Every tiger's stripe pattern is unique, and the stripes are in the skin as well as the fur.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
note: Two push blood through the gills and one serves the rest of the body, and that blood is blue because it uses copper rather than iron.

q: What does DNA stand for?
note: Its famous twisted-ladder shape is known as a double helix.

q: Which part of a living cell is known as its powerhouse, producing most of its energy?
note: They carry their own small, separate set of DNA, passed down only from the mother.

q: Which bird reaches the highest speed of any animal by diving on its prey?
note: In a full hunting dive it exceeds 300 kilometers an hour, faster than any other creature on Earth.

q: What is the largest living species of reptile?
note: Large males can exceed six meters and will happily swim far out to sea.

q: Which land animal has the longest pregnancy?
note: It lasts around 22 months, and the calf can weigh about 100 kilograms at birth.

q: What is the scientific study of insects called?
note: The word comes from a Greek term meaning cut into, a nod to an insect's segmented body.

q: A narwhal's long spiral tusk is actually an overgrown what?
note: It is a single canine that grows out through the animal's lip and is packed with nerve endings.

q: What is the name of the dance honeybees perform to tell the rest of the hive where food is?
note: The angle of the dance points toward the food and its length signals how far away it is.

q: Insects have no lungs, and instead take in air through small holes in their body called what?
note: Oxygen then reaches the tissues directly through a branching network of tubes, with no need for blood to carry it.

q: What is the term for the process in which an insect or a snake sheds its outer skin?
note: An insect's hard outer casing cannot stretch, so it has to be thrown away entirely for the animal to grow.

q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
note: The symbol comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.

q: What is the chemical formula for water?
note: The molecule is bent rather than straight, and that lopsided shape is what makes water such a good solvent.

q: Which metal has the chemical symbol Fe?
note: It comes from ferrum, the Latin name, which also gives us words like ferrous and farrier.

q: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance on Earth?
note: It is pure carbon, the same element as the soft graphite in a pencil, just packed together differently.

q: What is the chemical name for ordinary table salt?
note: In mineral form it is called halite, making it more or less the only rock that people routinely eat.

q: Which element is first on the periodic table and the lightest of them all?
note: It is also by far the most abundant element in the universe.

q: Which metal has the chemical symbol Pb?
note: It comes from the Latin plumbum, which is also the root of the word plumber.

q: Which is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature?
note: It was long known as quicksilver, and it is so dense that an iron ball will float on it.

q: What does the pH scale measure?
a: How acidic or alkaline something is
note: Seven is neutral, lower is acidic and higher is alkaline, and every single step is a tenfold change.

q: Which gas, the second lightest of all, is used to make party balloons float?
note: It was spotted in the light of the Sun in 1868, years before anyone managed to find any on Earth.

q: Which acid does the human stomach produce to help digest food?
note: It is strong enough to attack metal, so the stomach lining constantly renews itself to cope.

q: What is the term for a solid turning straight into a gas without becoming a liquid first?
note: Dry ice does exactly this at everyday temperatures, which is why it makes fog instead of a puddle.

q: What is the name for a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself?
note: The catalytic converter in a car uses precious metals this way to clean up exhaust gases.

q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
note: Copper is used for wiring instead purely because it is so much cheaper.

q: In the periodic table, what does an element's atomic number tell you?
a: The number of protons in its nucleus
note: Change the number of protons and you have changed the element itself, which is why they are ordered this way.

q: Which metal is extracted from the ore bauxite?
note: It was once more precious than gold, until cheap electricity made smelting it straightforward.

q: Which metal, prized for its extremely high melting point, has the chemical symbol W?
note: The symbol comes from its other name, wolfram, and it melts at a higher temperature than any other metal.

q: What name is given to the group of very unreactive gases in the far-right column of the periodic table?
note: Their outer electron shells are already full, so they have almost no interest in bonding with anything.

q: Which acid gives vinegar its sour taste and sharp smell?
note: Ordinary vinegar is only about five percent acetic acid, with the rest being mostly water.

q: Stainless steel is iron and carbon mixed with which other element to stop it rusting?
note: The chromium forms an invisible oxide layer that seals the surface and reforms whenever it is scratched.

q: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
note: It is more than twice as massive as every other planet in the solar system put together.

q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
note: The color comes from iron oxide in its soil, which is essentially rust.

q: What force pulls objects toward the center of the Earth?
note: It is by far the weakest of the fundamental forces, but unlike the others its reach is unlimited.

q: What is the nearest star to Earth?
note: The next nearest, Proxima Centauri, is more than four light years away.

q: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our solar system?
note: The hazy band you can see on a dark night is our own galaxy, viewed edge-on from the inside.

q: Which planet is famous for its bright system of rings?
note: The rings are made mostly of water ice and, despite spanning a vast width, are astonishingly thin.

q: What name is given to the distance light travels in one year?
note: It is a measure of distance rather than time, and works out at almost ten trillion kilometers.

q: Which English scientist set out the three laws of motion?
note: He published them in 1687 in the Principia, alongside his law of universal gravitation.

q: What is the name for the explosion of a massive star at the end of its life?
note: For a few weeks one can outshine the entire galaxy it sits in.

q: What is the term for heat travelling through a material by direct contact, such as a spoon warming in hot soup?
note: Metals do it well because their loosely held electrons ferry energy through the material quickly.

q: What is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another called?
note: It is exactly why a straw appears to snap in half at the surface of a glass of water.

q: What is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape called?
note: It is not a solid surface but a point of no return, where the speed needed to escape exceeds the speed of light.

q: Which is the hottest planet in our solar system?
note: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat so effectively that the surface is hot enough to melt lead.

q: What is it called when the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun?
note: It works so neatly because the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away.

q: Which property of a wave is measured in hertz?
note: One hertz is one cycle per second, named for Heinrich Hertz, who proved radio waves exist.

q: What is the name of the region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter where most asteroids are found?
note: Films make it look crowded, but the objects in it are so far apart that spacecraft sail straight through.

q: What is the name of the giant, long-lived storm on the surface of Jupiter?
note: Astronomers have been watching it for centuries, and it is still wider than the Earth.

q: What is the name for the change in a wave's pitch as its source moves toward or away from you?
note: It is why a siren drops in pitch the moment an ambulance passes you, and it also tells astronomers how galaxies are moving.

q: What is the point in a planet's orbit where it comes closest to the Sun called?
note: The opposite point, furthest from the Sun, is called aphelion.

q: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun because it is blown back by what?
note: That means a comet heading away from the Sun is actually travelling tail first.

q: What is molten rock called once it reaches the surface and flows out of a volcano?
note: The very same material is called magma while it is still underground.

q: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
note: It covers roughly a third of the planet's surface, which is more than all the land put together.

q: What is the name for a scientist who studies the weather?
note: The name has nothing to do with meteors, and comes from a Greek word for anything high in the sky.

q: What is the name for molten rock once it has reached the Earth’s surface?
note: The same material is called magma while it is still underground.

q: What is the main cause of the ocean's tides?
a: The gravitational pull of the Moon
note: The Sun tugs as well, and when the two line up you get the extra-large spring tides.

q: What is the name for a violently rotating column of air that reaches the ground?
note: When the same thing forms over water it is called a waterspout instead.

q: Which gas makes up roughly 78 percent of the Earth's atmosphere?
note: Oxygen accounts for about 21 percent, and everything else shares the small remainder.

q: What instrument is used to detect and record the shaking of an earthquake?
note: An early Chinese version, built in the second century, signalled a distant quake by dropping a ball from a dragon's mouth.

q: What type of rock is formed when molten rock cools and hardens?
note: The name comes from ignis, the Latin word for fire, and granite is a familiar example.

q: What is the Earth's thin, solid outermost layer called?
note: Beneath the oceans it can be as little as five kilometers thick, far thinner than under the continents.

q: What is the process called when water vapor cools and turns back into a liquid?
note: It is what forms clouds in the sky and beads of water on the outside of a cold glass.

q: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure?
note: A sharp fall in pressure usually means unsettled weather is on the way.

q: What is the theory that the Earth's outer shell is broken into large, slowly moving slabs called?
note: The plates creep along at roughly the speed your fingernails grow.

q: What name is given to the supercontinent that geologists believe existed around 250 million years ago?
note: It began breaking apart in the Jurassic, eventually producing the continents we have now.

q: Marble forms when limestone is heated and squeezed underground, making it which of the three main rock types?
note: The word means changed in form, and slate is made from shale in much the same way.

q: What is the name for a huge ocean wave set off by an undersea earthquake or landslide?
note: Out in deep water it can pass under a ship almost unnoticed, only rearing up as it reaches shallow coast.

q: What is the name of the towering, anvil-topped cloud that brings thunderstorms?
note: It can climb more than ten kilometers, flattening out at the top when it hits the ceiling of the lower atmosphere.

q: Which layer of the atmosphere contains the ozone layer?
note: It sits above almost all the weather, which is why airliners like to cruise at its lower edge.

q: What name is given to the ancient supercontinent in which today's landmasses were all joined together?
note: It began breaking apart roughly 175 million years ago, and the pieces are still drifting today.

q: What is the name of the scale used to rank the hardness of minerals, running from talc up to diamond?
note: It is a ranking rather than a measurement, so the gap between nine and ten is enormous.

q: Which physicist developed the theory of relativity?
note: His Nobel Prize was awarded not for relativity but for explaining the photoelectric effect.

q: Which Scottish bacteriologist discovered penicillin in 1928?
note: He noticed it by accident, when mold drifted into a dish he had left out while away on holiday.

q: What do the letters www stand for in a web address?
note: It was created at CERN, the particle physics laboratory, as a way for scientists to share documents.

q: Which naturalist set out the theory of evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species?
note: Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently, which is what finally pushed Darwin to publish.

q: The unit of power called the watt is named after which Scottish engineer?
note: His improvements to the steam engine in the 1770s made it efficient enough to power factories.

q: In computing, what does the abbreviation CPU stand for?
note: It is the part that actually carries out a program's instructions, one step after another.

q: Which scientist won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry?
note: She remains the only person ever to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

q: Which Russian chemist created the first widely accepted periodic table of the elements?
note: He left gaps for elements nobody had found yet, and correctly predicted what they would turn out to be like.

q: Which Italian astronomer discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter with an early telescope?
note: Watching objects circle something other than the Earth badly undermined the idea that everything revolved around us.

q: Which Austrian monk founded the study of genetics through experiments with pea plants?
note: His results were ignored for decades and only rediscovered around 1900, well after his death.

q: Who was granted the first United States patent for the telephone, in 1876?
note: A rival inventor, Elisha Gray, filed a competing claim at the same patent office on the very same day.

q: What does the word laser originally stand for?
a: Light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation
accept: Light amplification by the stimulated emission of radiation
note: The physics behind it was worked out in theory decades before the first working laser was built in 1960.

q: Who developed the first successful polio vaccine, announced in 1955?
note: Asked who held the patent, he replied that the people did, and never took a penny in royalties.

q: What does GPS stand for?
note: It times satellite signals so precisely that the system has to correct for the effects of relativity.

q: Which ancient Greek thinker is said to have leapt from his bath shouting Eureka?
note: The rule about floating bodies he is credited with still bears his name today.

q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957?
note: It was roughly the size of a beach ball and did nothing but transmit a steady radio beep.

q: Which German physicist discovered X-rays in 1895?
note: He received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery in 1901.

q: Which nineteenth-century mathematician is often called the first computer programmer?
note: Her notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine described how a machine could work through a sequence of steps.

q: Whose X-ray image, known as Photo 51, was crucial to working out the structure of DNA?
note: The photograph was produced in her laboratory at King's College London and showed the molecule's helical shape.

q: Which Swedish chemist invented dynamite and left his fortune to found a famous set of prizes?
note: A newspaper mistakenly ran his obituary while he was still alive, calling him a merchant of death.
